questions.stem: A 52-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of a low-grade fever, myalgia, productive cough, and skin lesions on his left upper back that developed during the previous week. He had a past medical history of poorly controlled diabetes (hemoglobin A1c 8.4) and hyperlipidemia. He was taking metformin, glipizide, aspirin, and atorvastatin. He smoked 1 pack per day (PPD) and drank alcohol occasionally. He was a chiropterologist (bat expert) and frequently explored caves. He was from Wisconsin and had returned recently from a 1 month-long trip to Grand Canyon in Arizona, Death Valley in California, and Four Corners. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C, heart rate was 90 beats/minute, blood pressure of 110/78 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 18 breaths/minute with SPO2 95% on room air. He had numerous erythematous plaques with minimal scaling and surrounding induration Investigations: CXR: normal appearances Skin biopsy: changes consistent with a squamous cell carcinoma Fungal cultures of skin biopsy: positive for mold after 14 days
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Blastomyces dermatitidis Epidemiology (from Wisconsin), skin involvement, and a culture positive for a mold is highly suggestive of disseminated blastomycosis. Skin lesions are a common presentation, commonly misidentified as squamous cell cancer on histopathology. The phenomenon is called pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia (PEH). His exposure (chiropterologist – study of bats) increases risk for histoplasmosis. However, skin lesions together with the presence of PEH are not consistent with it. Coccidioidomycosis is a likely possibility due to recent travel, but skin lesions in coccidioidomycosis are mostly on extremities and resemble erythema nodosum. It is also not a common cause of PEH. Skin findings are not consistent with Candida or Cryptococcus.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q2

questions.stem: A 24-year old man is referred for evaluation of chronic pneumonia. He has had multiple courses of antibacterial therapy and still has a significant left lower lobe consolidation as seen on his chest radiograph. An HIV test is negative. On chest CT , the area of consolidation was thought to be a mass-like lesion, and he was referred for biopsy. In the interim, he also developed multiple verrucous skin plaques. He undergoes a bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy and the pathology shows granulomas and broad-based budding yeast forms as shown in the image.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Blastomycosis Blastomycosis appears as broad-based budding yeast in tissue. Pulmonary blastomycosis can present as nonresolving pneumonia, cavitary pneumonia, or a mass-like lesion that can be confused with multiple other entities, including tuberculosis and lung cancer. Cutaneous lesions are the most common extrapulmonary manifestation of blastomycosis and typically appear as well-demarcated plaques or ulceronodular lesions. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q39

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presented with a painless, nonhealing skin lesion on her left foot, which developed over 4 weeks. She also described 2 months of fever, fatigue, and a dry cough, which had not responded to a short course of levofloxacin. She had no significant past medical history. She worked as a landscaper for the city park district in Chicago, Illinois. Investigations: CXR: left lower lobe infiltrate Bronchoscopy and skin biopsy were performed (GMS stain of transbronchial biopsy shown below):
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Itraconazole The patient lives in the Midwest and presents with chronic pneumonia and a skin lesion. She works as a landscaper with likely extensive soil exposure and potential for inhalation of fungal spores. The GMS stain shows large broadbased budding yeast forms consistent with Blastomyces dermatitidis. This patient has disseminated blastomycosis (pulmonary infection with cutaneous dissemination). She is clinically stable with no symptoms or signs noted that would be concerning for severe infection or CNS involvement. If she had severe infection a course of amphotericin B, preferably a lipid formulation, would be warranted. Itraconazole is the treatment of choice for mild to moderate forms of blastomycosis including nonsevere, disseminated infection. Fluconazole and the echinocandins are poorly active. Posaconazole has in vitro activity against Blastomyces, but clinical data are limited, and first-line therapy with this drug is not recommended. Prednisone should be avoided.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q14

What is the treatment for blastomycosis?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Tuberculosis; (2) Histoplasmosis. (Blastomycosis is a "great pretender" that mimics bacterial pneumonia, TB, and lung cancer.)
b) Severity-based: mild-to-moderate pulmonary/disseminated disease - itraconazole 200 mg PO (loaded 200 mg TID x3 days) once or twice daily for 6-12 months. Moderately severe-to-severe disease - liposomal amphotericin B 3-5 mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks (or until improvement), then itraconazole 200 mg PO once or twice daily for 6-12 months. Itraconazole is the drug of choice; fluconazole is less efficacious and reserved as an alternative.

cohort_answer.text: Other infections: Histoplasma; TB; Cocci. Treatment: Itraconazole; Ampho B; Fluconazole; Posaconazole.

parts_raw.text: Otherwise well. Skin bx shows budding yeast. Pathogen?
What other test(s) are indicated?
Treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Blastomyces dermatitidis - broad-based budding yeast; most cutaneous blastomycosis arises from hematogenous dissemination rather than direct inoculation, so pulmonary/systemic disease must be sought.
b) (1) Skin biopsy for fungal stain (GMS/PAS) and fungal culture; (2) Chest imaging (+/- CNS imaging if neurologic signs) to assess for pulmonary/disseminated disease; (3) Sputum/respiratory culture; (4) Urine Blastomyces antigen; (5) HIV testing to exclude immunocompromise.
c) Itraconazole 200 mg PO once or twice daily (load 200 mg TID x3 days) for 6-12 months for mild-to-moderate disease. If moderately severe/severe, liposomal amphotericin B 3-5 mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks followed by itraconazole for 6-12 months.

cohort_answer.text: A) Blastomyces dermatitidis (most skin manifestations from hematogenous spread, not direct inoculation). B) Skin biopsy and culture; chest imaging +/- CNS imaging; sputum culture (concurrent PNA); histopath from BAL (fungal stain/GMS); antigen testing; HIV testing. C) Itraconazole 200mg 1-2x/day x6-12 months for mild disseminated disease; if moderate-severe, AmphoB x1-2 weeks followed by Itraconazole x6-12 months.

parts.text: Name 2 other infections with the same presentation.
What is the treatment?

parts_raw.text: A) 2 other infections with same presentation
B) Treatment

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Tuberculosis; (2) Histoplasmosis. (Blastomycosis mimics bacterial pneumonia, TB, and malignancy; other endemic considerations include Nocardia/Actinomyces.)
b) Moderately severe-to-severe pulmonary blastomycosis: liposomal amphotericin B 3-5 mg/kg/day (or AmB deoxycholate 0.7-1 mg/kg/day) for 1-2 weeks or until improvement, then itraconazole 200 mg PO (loaded 200 mg TID x3 days) once or twice daily for 6-12 months. Mild-to-moderate disease: itraconazole alone for 6-12 months (check serum level at 2 weeks). Immunocompromised patients receive AmB induction then 12 months of itraconazole. In pregnancy use liposomal AmB and avoid teratogenic azoles.

cohort_answer.text: A) Most consistent with Blastomyces spp. pneumonia; other causes: TB, Histoplasma (also consider bronchogenic carcinoma, Nocardia, Actinomyces, melioidosis, parasitic like paragonimus). B) Pulmonary Blastomycosis - moderately severe to severe: lipid AmB 3-5mg/kg/day or AmB deoxycholate 0.7-1mg/kg/day x1-2 weeks or until improvement, followed by oral itraconazole 200mg TID x3d then 200mg BID x6-12 months. Mild to moderate: oral itraconazole 200mg TID x3d then OD/BID x6-12 months (check serum levels after 2 weeks). Immunosuppressed: lipid AmB 3-5mg/kg/d or AmB deoxycholate 0.7-1mg/kg/d x1-2 weeks, itraconazole 200mg TID x3d then BID x12 months, lifelong suppressive itraconazole 200mg/d may be needed if immunosuppression can't be reversed. Pregnant/children: lipid AmB (avoid azoles, teratogenic); newborn with infection - AmB deoxycholate 1mg/kg/d; children severe disease AmB then itraconazole 10mg/kg/d (max 400mg/d) x12 months; mild-moderate itraconazole 10mg/kg/d x6-12 months.

parts.text: Name 2 possible organisms.

parts_raw.text: A) Name 2 possible organisms

questions.model_answer: (1) Blastomyces dermatitidis; (2) Histoplasma capsulatum. Both are thermally dimorphic fungi (mould at 22-30 C, yeast at 37 C). Coccidioides is excluded by the absence of southwestern US exposure, and Paracoccidioides/Talaromyces are geographically inconsistent.

cohort_answer.text: Histoplasmosis; Blastomycosis. Dimorphic fungi grow as yeast in host, mold at room temperature in vitro; includes histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, chromoblastomycosis, adiaspiromycosis, and new Emmonsia/Emergomyces/Talaromyces agents. Mnemonic: 'Mold in the Cold, Yeast in the Heat'.

parts.text: Identify the most likely pathogen on the following illustrations.

parts_raw.text: Identify the most likely pathogen on the following illustrations

questions.model_answer: (1) Blastomyces dermatitidis — 8-15 um round multinucleated broad-based budding yeast (large pore, daughter cell attached until near mother's size). (2) Aspergillus spp. — 2-5 um septate hyphae of even diameter with acute-angle (Y-shaped, dichotomous) branching; propensity for vascular invasion. (3) Pneumocystis jirovecii — 3.5-7 um nonbudding cup/cysts, black on GMS with central dot, clustered in alveoli in eosinophilic amorphous material. Contrast with agents of mucormycosis — 4-15 um-wide, rarely septate hyphae of uneven diameter branching at broad (near 90-degree) angles.

cohort_answer.text: Blastomyces (broad-based budding yeast); Aspergillus (septate with acute angle branching); Pneumocystis jiroveci. Remember - mucor (thicker aseptate, 90 degree branching).

questions.question_raw: Q19 (2014). Pictures of respiratory specimens, and asked to identify: [image-based question: histopathology images of respiratory fungal pathogens]

parts.text: Identify the organisms shown in the histopathology images.

parts_raw.text: Identify the organisms shown in the histopathology images

questions.model_answer: Distinguish by tissue morphology (Table 255.2): (1) Coccidioides posadasii/immitis — 5-60 um thick-walled, nonbudding round spherules containing endospores; cavities may contain hyphae. (2) Blastomyces dermatitidis — 8-15 um round multinucleated yeast with broad-based bud (large pore, daughter attached until nearly mother's size); pyogenic and granulomatous inflammation. (3) Aspergillus spp. — 2-5 um-wide, frequently septate hyphae of even diameter with acute-angle Y-shaped branching; vascular invasion and necrosis. (4) Pneumocystis jirovecii — 3.5-7 um nonbudding cysts staining black on GMS (may show central black dot), white on calcofluor, in clusters within alveoli surrounded by eosinophilic amorphous material. (5) Talaromyces marneffei — 2-3 x 2-6 um oblong intracellular yeasts, some with a central cross-septum (division by fission, not budding).

cohort_answer.text: Coccidioides immitis: necrotizing/suppurative granulomatous inflammation, large (20-200 micron) thick-walled spherules with basophilic endospores (2-4 microns), eosinophilic infiltrate common, occasional thin septate hyphae with arthroconidia (esp diabetics). Talaromyces marneffei: (formerly Penicillium marneffei) - endemic to SE Asia/southern China/eastern India, usually with immunodeficiency; intracytoplasmic organisms similar to histoplasma, sausage cells with light blue cytoplasm and central cross walls (fission not budding), 1-2 purple-red nuclei. Blastomyces dermatitidis: mixed acute/granulomatous inflammation, large budding yeasts (8-15 micron) with broad-based buds and refractile walls, easily seen on H&E. Aspergillosis: dichotomous branching (45 degree angle) septate hyphae, 2.5-4.5 micron diameter, may see fruiting body, often invades vessels. Pneumocystis jirovecii: alveolar spaces filled with pink foamy amorphous material (proliferating fungi and debris), 4-6 micron cup/boat shaped cysts, mild inflammatory reaction with fibrin exudate/hyaline membranes; can rarely cause necrotizing granulomas/miliary disease.
